commit.message:
gthread: keep kept-alive connections briefly when the worker stops

When a worker stopped (max_requests, reload, SIGTERM) it closed its
kept-alive connections at once, including one whose response had just
announced keep-alive while another thread reached max_requests. A
client reusing the connection, such as one following a redirect, lost
the request it was sending.

A stopping worker now keeps these connections for up to 2 seconds
(STOP_KEEPALIVE_LINGER, or their keepalive timeout if shorter) and
answers a request arriving on one with "Connection: close" (RFC 9112
section 9.6). The wait stays short so long keepalive timeouts do not
hold a stopping worker, which 814a3c2a addressed.

Fixes #3821

commit.message:
asgi: keep waiting for a call that left request body unread

Once the next request is read, the previous request's unread body no
longer counts towards the read backpressure, so up to 16 of them could
be held per connection. Serve the next request early only when the app
has taken the whole body.

tests: background tasks in the Starlette and FastAPI compat apps

Each app gets a /background endpoint that answers and then runs a sync
background task, the pattern from #3819. The test checks that the next
request on the same connection is answered without waiting for the
task, and that the task still finishes.

asgi: serve the next keep-alive request once the response is complete

The HTTP/1 connection loop awaited the application call before reading
the next request, so anything the app did after its last response
message, such as Starlette and FastAPI background tasks, held up every
request behind it on the same connection.

The call now runs in its own task. Once its response is complete, the
connection can be kept alive and the request body was read in full,
the loop moves on while the call finishes. Otherwise, or when a
post_request hook is set (it runs after the call and may still close
the connection), it waits for the call as before. At most 16 such
calls run per connection; the keepalive timer starts only when the
last one ends, so the connection lives as long as before, and on
disconnect they get http.disconnect and asgi_disconnect_grace_period
like the current request.

Fixes #3819

asgi: refuse a 1xx response sent after the final response started

An http.response.informational sent after http.response.start was
written to the transport straight away, ahead of the buffered final
headers or inside the body. RFC 9110 section 15.2: a 1xx comes before
the final response. Treat it like the other out-of-order messages.

commit.message:
agents: list the HTTP/1 framing rules and how CI runs pylint

The RFC 9112 row now names the sections gunicorn enforces (line
endings, Transfer-Encoding framing, chunked coding and extensions).
CI runs pylint 3.3.2 under Python 3.12, which reports warnings a 3.13
run does not; give the command that reproduces it.

docs: describe the ASGI worker's request handling and performance

Add what a client sees from the worker: Expect: 100-continue, 400 for
a malformed request or a Transfer-Encoding not ending with chunked,
501 for an unknown coding, 414 and 431 for the limits, and the reason
phrase. Point to the benchmark in benchmarks/asgi with the measured
results, and say that both parsers accept and reject the same requests.

Also correct two stale claims: HTTP/2 does not do server push, and it
works over cleartext h2c behind a trusted proxy, not only over TLS.

docs: sort the unreleased changelog into breaking changes, fixes and changes

The entries added over the last pull requests were long single lines
filed under Bug Fixes. Group them as the earlier releases do: the
Transfer-Encoding rule under Breaking Changes, the fixes in the usual
short wrapped form, and the performance work and the gunicorn_h1c
requirement under Changes, one line each instead of five separate
version bumps.

commit.message:
build: require gunicorn_h1c 0.6.14

gunicorn_h1c 0.6.14 does what gunicorn's Python parsers now do: it
checks the whole chunk extension grammar, accepts BWS before the first
';', rejects a Transfer-Encoding that does not end with chunked, and
raises UnsupportedTransferCoding for an unknown coding, which gunicorn
answers with 501 on both workers.

The expected failures for gunicorn_h1c are gone, and the two corpus
cases for Transfer-Encoding run against it too. The check after
parsing in CallbackRequest.from_parser() stays, since the floor is not
enforced at runtime.

lint: put the two pylint disables where CI reports them

The isinstance() warning is reported on the line that opens the call,
and the return count on _feed_callback_parser(), which gained the 501
branch. Checked with pylint 3.3.2 under Python 3.12, as CI runs it.

lint: silence two pylint false positives seen under Python 3.12

CI's pylint, without gunicorn_h1c installed, cannot tell that the
UnsupportedTransferCoding class read with getattr() is a type, and
counts one return too many in _handle_h1c_exception().

asgi, http: answer 501 to an unknown transfer coding on every path

RFC 9112 section 6.1: a transfer coding the server does not understand
SHOULD get 501. The WSGI Python parser answers 501; the ASGI worker
answered 400 for the same request, with either parser.

The ASGI worker now maps the Python parser's UnsupportedTransferCoding
to 501. gunicorn_h1c raises a plain InvalidHeader for now; once it
raises its own UnsupportedTransferCoding, the ASGI worker and the WSGI
fast path answer 501 for it too.

http, asgi: reject a Transfer-Encoding that does not end with chunked

RFC 9112 section 6.3: when a request's Transfer-Encoding does not end
with chunked, its length cannot be determined, and the server MUST
answer 400 and close. gunicorn accepted 'gzip', 'identity' and the
like alone: the WSGI parser read the body until the connection closed
(the rule for responses), the ASGI parsers framed it as empty, so the
same request was framed two ways.

All parsers now answer 400. gunicorn_h1c 0.6.13 still frames it as
empty, so CallbackRequest.from_parser() checks it after parsing, as it
does for repeated singleton fields.

tests/requests/valid/009.http (Transfer-Encoding: identity with
Content-Length) moves to the invalid corpus: nginx and Go answer 501,
Node, Apache, h11 and llhttp reject it too.

asgi: accept whitespace before the first ';' of a chunk size line

RFC 9112 section 7.1.1 allows BWS before every ';' of a chunk
extension, the first one included: '1 ;a'. The WSGI parser accepts it;
the ASGI Python parser rejected it as whitespace in the chunk size.

The size may now be followed by SP or HTAB when an extension comes
next. Whitespace with no extension after it, or before the size, is
still rejected. gunicorn_h1c still rejects this form; its cases are
marked as expected failures until it accepts them.

commit.message:
asgi: take error reason phrases from gunicorn's table first

HTTPStatus phrases change between Python versions: 414 is
'Request-URI Too Long' before 3.13 and 'URI Too Long' after. Error
responses now use the same table as application responses, and
HTTPStatus only for codes it lacks, so the status line does not depend
on the Python version.

http, asgi: check the chunk extension grammar in the Python parsers

Apart from a bare CR, anything after the ';' of a chunk size line was
accepted: control characters, DEL, an unclosed quote, an empty name,
separators inside a name. RFC 9112 section 7.1.1 allows only
';' token ['=' (token / quoted-string)], with optional whitespace
around ';' and '='.

Both Python parsers now match the extension against that grammar and
answer 400 otherwise. The size is still checked first, so a bad size
keeps its own error. gunicorn_h1c does not check the grammar yet; its
cases are marked as expected failures until it does.

http, asgi: reject a bare LF at once in the Python parsers

RFC 9112 section 2.2: lines end with CRLF; gunicorn_h1c rejects a bare
LF wherever it ends a line. The Python parsers only rejected it where
it left something invalid behind (a header line, a chunk size). A head
or trailer section ended by a bare LF, or a request using LF alone,
kept the connection waiting for a CRLF until limit_request_line, the
header buffer limit or the timeout.

The ASGI Python parser checks for an LF before the next CRLF where it
looks for every line end; the WSGI parser does the same for the
request line and while it waits for the end of the head or of the
trailers. All three parsers now reject the same requests with 400.

asgi: keep the error text out of the status line

_send_error_response() wrote its message as the reason phrase:
'HTTP/1.1 400 Invalid character ... in header name'. The message often
quotes the request, so request bytes ended up in the status line, and
a message outside latin-1 made the encode fail.

The status line now carries the standard reason phrase for the code
and the message goes only in the body, as the WSGI workers already do
(RFC 9112 section 4).

asgi: answer 400 to every request gunicorn_h1c rejects

Only three gunicorn_h1c errors were handled: the two limits and the
invalid chunk extension. Every other rejection (duplicate Host, space
before the colon, obs-fold, Content-Length with Transfer-Encoding, bad
method or version, bare LF, bad chunk size, ...) escaped data_received.
The event loop then logged a traceback and dropped the connection with
no response, once per bad request, where RFC 9112 asks for a 400 and
the Python parser sends one.

gunicorn_h1c raises two unrelated ParseError classes, the public one
and one from H1CProtocol; both now get a 400 and the connection is
closed.

commit.message:
build: require gunicorn_h1c 0.6.12

gunicorn_h1c 0.6.12 decoded chunked bodies in quadratic time before:
a 64 KiB chunked body took about 23 times as long as the same body with
Content-Length. It also parses without copying the input and measures
the request line after the allowed empty line in parse_request().

Its H1CProtocol now calls on_body once per feed() with all the chunk
data that call decoded; gunicorn's body receiver already handled
chunks of any size, and the suite passes unchanged on it.

http: check limit_request_line after the empty line on the fast path

RFC 9112 section 2.2 lets one empty line come before the request line.
gunicorn_h1c before 0.6.12 did not measure the request line after it,
so with the fast parser the WSGI workers accepted a request line over
limit_request_line when it was preceded by CRLF; the Python parser
answered 414.

The fast path now measures the request line itself when the request
starts with that empty line, as _parse_python() does. Requests without
it do not pay for the check. The ASGI worker's parser (H1CProtocol)
already measured it correctly.

ASGI: cheaper requests and responses

commit.message:
bench: record the results of the request and response work

Interleaved against master fb3de7ee, 5 rounds, one worker. The native
worker with gunicorn_h1c as a share of Uvicorn: small GET 89% -> 95%,
30 extra headers 71% -> 82%, streamed response 63% -> 89%, 1 MiB
response 83% -> 92%; peak RSS on the large and streamed responses
146 MB -> 95 MB.

asgi: copy a bytearray or memoryview body before sending it

A body chunk after the first went to the transport as the app gave it,
and a transport that cannot send at once keeps the object it was given.
An app that reused a bytearray (or a memoryview of one) once send()
returned changed bytes that were still waiting to go out. A body that
is not bytes is now copied to bytes when sent; bytes bodies, which the
ASGI spec asks for, are unaffected.

asgi: write each body chunk with one call, the last with its terminator

A body chunk went through send(), _send_body() and _safe_write() before
reaching the transport, and the chunked terminator of a streamed
response was a write of its own. _send_body() now writes directly, with
the same error handling, and the last chunk carries the terminator, so
a streamed response makes one write fewer (one send system call). The
bytes on the wire are unchanged. Calls per /stream request (16 chunks):
284 -> 262 (Uvicorn 205); in process 44 us against Uvicorn's 41.

asgi: skip the default pre_request hook when it would not log

The default pre_request hook only logs the method and path at debug
level, yet it ran on every request with debug logging off. The protocol
now decides once per connection: with the default hook, gunicorn's
Logger (or the StatsD one) and debug logging off, it calls nothing. A
custom hook, a custom logger class or debug logging keep the call, so
nothing that could be seen changes.

asgi: await the write drain only while writing is paused

Every body chunk of a streamed response awaited FlowControl.drain(),
a coroutine that only waits on an event, and that event is set whenever
writing is not paused. The protocol now checks write_paused first and
awaits only then, which is the same behaviour without one coroutine and
one Event.wait() per chunk. Calls per /stream request (16 chunks):
300 -> 284.

asgi: send large response bodies without copying them

The first body chunk was joined to the buffered headers, and a chunk of
a chunked response was joined to its size line and CRLF (twice). The
join copied the body; for a 1 MiB response each connection then held
its own 1 MiB copy until the socket took it, which is where most of
the extra RSS against Uvicorn under load came from.

A body of 64 KiB or more now goes to transport.writelines() next to
its framing, so the transport sends the app's own bytes object. Smaller
bodies are still joined (once, for chunks) into one write. The bytes on
the wire are unchanged. Peak memory per 1 MiB response, in process:
1033 KiB -> 10 KiB (Uvicorn 7.6 KiB).

bench: profile streamed and 1 MiB responses

The in-process profiler only knew small responses. It now also drives
/stream (16 chunks of 4 KiB) and /large (1 MiB), so the response path
can be measured the same way as the request path.

asgi: build the str copy of request headers only when read

Every request decoded and upper-cased each header into a second list,
though serving it needs only the bytes ASGI hands to the app. With 30
extra headers that copy was 37% of the profiled time per request.

The copy is now built the first time something reads request.headers
(hooks, access log, WebSocket and h2c handshakes). The header policy
works on the bytes, and the Connection and Upgrade facts it needed are
noted in from_parser()'s single pass. Once the str headers have been
read, they are scanned as before, so a hook that edits them is still
seen. Calls per request: 138 -> 121 (small GET), 306 -> 121 (30 extra
headers; Uvicorn 174).

commit.message:
asgi: answer Expect: 100-continue on HTTP/1.1

The worker recorded the expectation but never sent the 100, so a
client holding its body back (curl on large uploads) waited for its own
timeout, about a second, before sending it.

Send "100 Continue" when the app first asks for a body the client has
not sent yet, as the HTTP/2 path and Uvicorn do. No 100 goes out when
the app answers first, when the body came with the headers, when there
is no body, or for HTTP/1.0, where the expectation must be ignored
(RFC 9110 section 10.1.1).

commit.message:
bench: record the results of the ASGI overhead work

head-vs-master compares the branch with master on every workload;
step*-vs-* gate each commit against the one before, interleaved.
OVERHEAD.md summarizes them: small GET +23.5% with gunicorn_h1c (86% of
Uvicorn, from 69%) and +27.7% with the Python parser.

asgi: prepare the response with fewer passes

Every response rebuilt the 60-entry reason-phrase dict to look up a
phrase the status-line cache did not need, then went over the response
headers twice before serializing them: once to validate them, once to
find Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding.

Keep the reason phrases in a module-level table, looked up only the
first time a (version, status) is seen, and validate the headers in the
same pass that finds their framing, still before the response counts as
started so an invalid header is still a 500. The bytes written are
unchanged for a matrix of responses (statuses, str and bytes headers,
app and server chunking, HEAD, HTTP/1.0, invalid header), recorded from
the previous code as a test.

Calls per request (in process, small GET): gunicorn_h1c 141 -> 137.
Measured, interleaved against the previous commit (7 rounds, small GET,
req/s median): +5.7% with gunicorn_h1c, +6.7% with the Python parser,
close to the run-to-run spread (4-8%).

asgi: build the request in one pass over its headers

CallbackRequest.from_parser() went over the parser's headers three times
(str copy, singleton check, Expect) and percent-decoded every path, and
the header policy then called its full per-field check on every header.

Build the str copy, the singleton check and the Expect flag in one pass;
skip unquote when the path has no '%' (the result is the same); run the
policy check only on fields it can act on (scheme headers and names with
'_'), the singleton fields being checked by from_parser() already. The
request is the same field for field (tested against the previous code for
both parsers). The Expect flag now also sees gunicorn_h1c's mixed-case
names; nothing reads it today.

Calls per request (in process, gunicorn_h1c): small GET 147 -> 141;
30 extra headers 382 -> 309.
Measured, interleaved against the previous commit (7 rounds, req/s
median): 30 extra headers +5.9% with gunicorn_h1c, +1.2% with the Python
parser; small GET within noise (+0.5%, -0.2%).

asgi: read per-request settings once per connection

Each request on the native ASGI worker resolved 17 settings through
Config.__getattr__ (keepalive four times, the access-log switch reading
six settings, the hooks, root_path, protocol, proxy_protocol) and parsed
the peer address with ipaddress to decide whether it may set forwarded
headers.

None of these can change during a connection: a configuration reload
starts new workers. Read them in ASGIProtocol.__init__, decide the
forwarded-header trust on the first request of a connection, and compute
Logger.access_log_enabled in setup(), which a reload runs. Request
values (forwarded header contents, scheme, worker.alive, counters) stay
per request.

Config reads per request: 17 -> 0. Calls per request (in process, small
GET): gunicorn_h1c 214 -> 147, Python parser 264 -> 197.
Measured, one worker, interleaved against the previous commit (7 rounds,
small GET, req/s median): gunicorn_h1c 42007 -> 53159 (+26.5%), Python
parser 37571 -> 45058 (+19.9%).

commit.message:
Add an ASGI benchmark harness and a baseline

The scripts used to compare the native ASGI worker with Uvicorn were not
in the repository, defaulted to the pure-Python parser and four workers,
and derived per-request costs from 1/RPS under concurrency.

benchmarks/asgi/ runs gunicorn's native worker (gunicorn_h1c and Python
parser), Uvicorn and gunicorn with Uvicorn's worker on the same app with
matched settings, warmed up, in alternating rounds, and records req/s,
p50/p95/p99, errors, server and client CPU and peak RSS with the exact
environment. --baseline-root runs another revision interleaved in the
same rounds. profile_requests.py measures the Python cost of one request
in process (time, calls, memory, cProfile), separately from throughput.

results/ holds the baseline for master (6a0a716a) against 5be13466 and
Uvicorn; BASELINE.md summarizes it.

Merge pull request #3805 from benoitc/fix/review-findings

Bound buffers and follow RFC 6455 / ASGI in the ASGI, HTTP/2, WebSocket and dirty paths

commit.message:
dirty: time out every stream read and drop the connection on timeout

The async stream iterator read without any timeout while more than 5 s
were left before the total deadline, so a stalled stream ignored its idle
timeout and the deadline alike. The sync iterator used a fixed 5 s socket
timeout in that case, replacing the configured idle timeout. Neither
closed the connection on timeout, so the rest of an abandoned stream was
read by the next call as its own reply.

Bound every read by min(time left, idle timeout) in both iterators, and
close the connection when it fires. The async bound costs about 1.6 us
per chunk on an in-memory stream (539k -> 304k chunks/s), small next to
the IPC each chunk goes through.

websocket: raise an OSError on send after close

ASGI 2.4 says send() on a closed connection should raise a
server-specific subclass of OSError, and servers should not log it as an
error. The WebSocket raised a plain RuntimeError, logged as an
application error when it escaped. Raise WebSocketDisconnected, a
subclass of both ClientDisconnected (OSError) and RuntimeError, so code
catching either keeps working, and log it at debug level only.

HTTP/1 sends after a disconnect stay silently ignored, as before and as
other ASGI servers do; HTTP/2 already raised ClientDisconnected.

websocket: apply write backpressure

websocket.send wrote frames straight to the transport and never waited
on the connection's flow control, so an application streaming to a slow
client grew the transport's write buffer past its high-water mark. Give
the WebSocket the connection's FlowControl.drain and wait on it before
each text or binary message, as HTTP responses do. Control frames (close,
ping, pong) are not held back, so a close handshake never waits on it.

websocket: refuse an unaccepted handshake with HTTP 403

websocket.close before websocket.accept wrote a WebSocket close frame on
a connection that had not switched protocols, then waited 5 seconds for a
reply that could not come; an app that returned or raised without
accepting left the request unanswered. The ASGI WebSocket spec says the
server must answer HTTP 403 and not complete the handshake. Do that for
a close before accept or an app that returns without accepting, and
answer 500 when it raised.

websocket: check version and key in the handshake

Any GET with Upgrade: websocket was upgraded, whatever its
Sec-WebSocket-Version and Sec-WebSocket-Key. RFC 6455 section 4.2.1
requires version 13 and a key that base64-decodes to 16 bytes. Answer
another version with 426 and Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13 (section 4.2.2),
and a missing or malformed key with 400. Browsers and WebSocket libraries
always send both.

websocket: enforce RFC 6455 frame rules

The reader accepted a new text or binary frame in the middle of a
fragmented message (overwriting it), ignored reserved opcodes, did not
check that lengths are minimally encoded with the top bit clear, echoed
any close code back (1005 included) and decoded close reasons leniently.
A text message that was not UTF-8 dropped the connection without a close
frame.

Fail the connection as RFC 6455 says: 1002 for interleaved messages,
reserved opcodes, bad lengths, a one-byte close body or a code a peer may
not send (sections 5.2, 5.4, 5.5.1, 7.4); 1007 for text or a close
reason that is not UTF-8 (section 8.1). A valid close is echoed as
before; an empty one is answered with 1000.

http2: cap events set aside while waiting for window credit

While a sync worker waited for WINDOW_UPDATE, every frame not about its
stream was set aside for the main loop in a queue with no limit, and with
timeout = 0 the wait has no deadline. A peer withholding window credit
and sending frames grew it without end. Past 10000 events, close the
connection with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM.

http2: cap PING, SETTINGS and empty DATA frames

Only RST_STREAM had a rate limit; a peer could send PING, SETTINGS or
empty DATA frames without end, each costing work and carrying no request.
Count them per connection like resets: more than 1000 in 10 seconds
closes the connection with GOAWAY(ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM). On the sync worker,
PING and SETTINGS seen while waiting for window credit are counted there
and no longer set aside, since the main loop does nothing with them.

The live test that kept a connection usable after 20,000 PINGs now
expects the GOAWAY; a new one checks 500 PINGs leave it serving. The h2c
reader test fills the buffer with WINDOW_UPDATE frames instead of PINGs.

asgi: bound the HTTP/1 request body buffer

Body chunks an application had not received piled up in a list with no
limit, and reading from the socket was never paused for HTTP/1 (only the
HTTP/2 reader was checked). Draining the list with pop(0) was quadratic,
the pure-Python parser kept a pipelined tail uncapped, and the uWSGI path
read the whole body before starting the application.

Keep chunks in a deque with a byte count, pause reading while more than
256 KiB of body or pipelined data waits, and resume as the application
reads. uWSGI bodies are read as the application asks for them; what it
leaves is drained before the next request. Applications reading their
body see the same bytes in the same order.

commit.message:
asgi_compliance: count requests with a mutable object in lifespan state

Since #3791 each request gets a shallow copy of the lifespan state, as the
ASGI lifespan spec requires, so an integer bumped in scope["state"] no
longer carries over to the next request. The test app relied on the old
shared dict; keep a counter dict in the state at startup and increment it
in place, which is how state is meant to be shared.

commit.message:
WSGI: answer 500 when the application sends an invalid response header

Response header validation raised InvalidHeader / InvalidHeaderName,
which handle_error() maps to 400 and logs as an invalid request from the
client. Raise InvalidResponseHeader / InvalidResponseHeaderName instead
(subclasses, so existing except clauses still match) and treat them as an
application error: 500, logged with the traceback. The error names the
header only, never its value.

Close the connection after a CONNECT request

RFC 9931 section 8 requires a server rejecting a CONNECT to close the
connection without processing further requests: the client may already be
forwarding tunnel data, which would otherwise be read as a new HTTP/1.1
request (its Figure 1 attack served a pipelined POST on master, WSGI and
ASGI). gunicorn hands CONNECT to the application and cannot tunnel, so a
CONNECT now always ends the connection, on both WSGI parsers and on the
ASGI worker. AGENTS.md and the review skill record what RFC 9931 asks.

commit.message:
Read chunked request bodies in large steps

The chunked reader read chunk data with a bare unreader.read(), one
recv(8192) at a time, although each chunk header says how many bytes
follow. Pass what is left of the chunk as the read hint, so the socket
reads up to that much (at most 1 MiB) in one call and never past the end
of the chunk.

64 MiB body, median MiB/s with three CPU-bound threads: 1 MiB chunks
17.7 -> 26.4 (read()) and 7.3 -> 26.0 (read(65536)); 64 KiB chunks
13.6 -> 25.4 and 10.4 -> 18.5. Idle, 1 MiB chunks read() 1687 -> 7778.

Fixes #2596

Merge pull request #3799 from benoitc/fix/dirty-pidfile-hardening

Harden the dirty arbiter PID file

commit.message:
Harden the dirty arbiter PID file

The dirty arbiter writes its PID to a well-known path in the temporary
directory, and a new master reads it to stop an arbiter left behind by a
crash. The file was written with open() and read back without any check,
so a file someone else placed there could make gunicorn signal any
process the user can signal.

Write it with O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW and mode 0600, replacing only a
stale file this user owns. Before stopping an orphan, require a regular
file owned by this user and not writable by group or others, and on Linux
a process owned by this user. Untrusted files are logged and left alone.

commit.message:
Reject raw non-ASCII bytes in the request-target: code and tests

The previous commit only moved valid/027 to the invalid corpus; this one
carries the change it describes. The request-target check now refuses
anything outside printable ASCII (RFC 9112 section 3.2, RFC 3986 section
2) on the WSGI and ASGI paths and in the shared ASGI backstop.

Reject raw non-ASCII bytes in the request-target

RFC 9112 section 3.2 builds the request-target from the URI grammar of
RFC 3986, whose characters are printable ASCII (section 2); any other
octet must be percent-encoded (section 2.1). Every parser accepted raw
bytes 0x80-0xFF in the path. Extend the existing control-character check to
anything outside 0x21-0x7E, on the WSGI and ASGI paths and in the backstop
both ASGI parsers share. valid/027 (raw UTF-8 path) moves to the invalid
corpus.

commit.message:
Join repeated request headers once when building the WSGI environ

Each repeated header was appended to the environ value with a new string,
copying the growing value every time, so many copies of one header took
time growing with the square of their number (bounded by
limit_request_fields). Collect the values and join them once: 32768 copies
go from 774 ms to 4 ms. The resulting environ is unchanged.

commit.message:
Skip the body memory test on PyPy

It measures allocations with tracemalloc, which PyPy does not provide.

Changelog: request bodies read in large steps

Measured with a 64 MiB body over a socket pair: wsgi.input.read() goes
from 807 to 8724 MiB/s idle and from 2.4 to 49 MiB/s with three CPU-bound
threads in the process; read(65536) from 791 to 3241 and from 8 to 46.

http: read request bodies in large steps

Body.read() asked its reader for 1 KiB at a time, and LengthReader pushed
the rest of each received chunk back with unread(), copying it again on
every call. SocketUnreader never called recv() with more than 8 KiB.

Every recv() releases the GIL, so with other busy threads in the worker a
large body was read at a few MiB/s at best. Body.read() now asks for what
is still missing, in steps of at most 1 MiB, and recv() reads up to 1 MiB
while a body of known length is being read, never past its end. Peak
memory of a whole-body read() is unchanged.

Fixes #2596

Claude helped investigate the issue and write the PR description.

commit.message:
sock: listen() when SO_ACCEPTCONN cannot be read, tidy whitespace

getsockopt(SO_ACCEPTCONN) can raise on a platform that defines the
constant without supporting it for that socket; fall back to listen() as
before instead of failing to start. Remove trailing whitespace pycodestyle
rejects, and add the changelog lines for the socket and StatsD fixes.

add tests
make sure that reuse socket only when socket package supports it

fix: avoid re-listening on inherited sockets

We run Gunicorn in podman containers with SELinux and we noticed the
process skips bind call correctly but then calls listen when systemd
socket activation is enabled. This is not needed since systemd already
calls bind/listen for the managed process.

The call cannot be simply skipped, because this would break the current
behavior on sockets passed via `--bind`. Therefore, the call is only
skipped when socket is already in listening (SO_ACCEPTCONN).

Merge pull request #3793 from benoitc/fix/gthread-keepalive

gthread keepalive fixes and close on body read errors

commit.message:
Close the connection when reading a request body fails

An error while reading a request body, such as a repeated singleton field
in chunked trailers, could lose bytes already read ahead from the socket
while the connection stayed alive, so the next read started in the wrong
place. The trailer reader now hands those bytes back before checking the
trailers, a body that raised is marked failed, and finish_body() refuses
keepalive for it. The parser stops instead of reading the next request
when the previous body could not be finished. Add the changelog lines for
the gthread fixes.

gthread/ThreadWorker/graceful shutdown: don't wait for idle keepalive conns

If you are running behind a loadbalancer and have enabled long keepalives
(e.g.: 60s), with the default graceful restart timeout of 30s, a worker
with only keepalive conns will wait the full timeout before restarting.
Given that a previously used idle connection would have been prematurely
terminated when the worker was SIGABRTed, there's no change in behaviour
to downstream clients... we just avoid shooting ourselves.
